newsitem.title: GERMANY: Trial opens of Germans accused of racist attack.
newsitem.headline: Trial opens of Germans accused of racist attack.

text.p: Two German men accused of carrying out a racially-motivated attack on three black Britons which left one of them seriously injured said at the start of their trial on Monday that they were fans of action and horror films.

Mario Poetter, 24, and Sandro Ristau, 18, have been charged with causing grievous bodily harm and recklessly driving a vehicle in a high-speed pursuit of the British construction workers that led to a serious car crash last June.
"I like action films and horror films," Poetter said under questioning from Judge Klaus Przybilla. Ristau told the court he was a fan of Arnold Schwarzenegger films.

One of the British workers, Noel Martin, was paralysed from the neck down when the car he was riding in crashed into a tree after the two Germans, shouting racial epithets, threw a rock through the car window.
Judge Klaus Przybilla told the court on Monday that the two could also be convicted of attempted murder.

The attack in Mahlow, a small village south of Berlin, came during a wave of violence in eastern Germany during the summer in which gangs of youths toting baseball bats and iron bars have besieged camp sites.
Poetter and Ristau admitted to shouting "nigger" at the construction workers at a local train station before pursuing them. They also admitted hurling a rock through the rear window of the car.
But the accused claim the crash occurred when the three Britons attempted to chase after them after they had thrown the rock, which led to a collision with a tree and Martin's subsequent injuries.
The two young men have told police that they belong to the local neo-Nazi circles in Mahlow. But they denied belonging to any organised hate group.

Another trial of an 18-year-old for the murder of another British construction worker, Lee Hawthorn, in September 1994 opened last week. The German, identified only as Steffen H., is accused of tying Hawthorn to his car and dragging him over eight km (5 miles) behind the car.

Eastern Germany, a region with high unemployment, has witnessed many high-profile attacks against foreigner workers this year, reviving memories of the extremist violence immediately after German unification in 1990.
